forces: Orchestra with piano, celesta and two harps
performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet
intro: Evening brings nursemaids, coachmen and a performing bear back to the fair; then Petrushka’s quarrel spills out of the puppet theatre. The crowd goes home, snow falls, and two muted trumpets give the dead puppet the last laugh.

cues.title: Evening at the fair
cues.text: The drums roll again and the curtain opens on the fair at dusk. The crowd’s dance returns in winds, brass and strings. The two cramped puppet rooms are behind us; the stage fills with people.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe full score, plate R.M.V. 127, pp. 96–103, rehearsals 82–89; original fourth-tableau setting transcribed in Kirchmeyer, K012. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A puppet with a piano
cues.text: In Switzerland in 1910 Stravinsky composes a concerto-like piece for piano and orchestra: a puppet, suddenly alive, cavorts up the keyboard until the orchestra explodes. It ends, he writes, in “the sorrowful and querulous collapse of the poor puppet.” Diaghilev visits, expecting sketches for The Rite, hears the puppet instead and urges a ballet.
cues.evidence: Stravinsky, An Autobiography (New York: Simon & Schuster, 1936), pp. 47–48, in the Internet Archive scan https://archive.org/details/stravinskyautobi00stra : the piece with a leading piano, the puppet “suddenly endowed with life”, “the sorrowful and querulous collapse of the poor puppet”, and Diaghilev’s visit to Clarens. Steven Ledbetter’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note describes it as a concerto-like piece for piano and orchestra and places the composition at Lausanne and Clarens between August 1910 and May 1911: https://www.bso.org/works/stravinsky-petrushka-1947-version

cues.title: The nursemaids’ song
cues.text: Bassoons bustle above plucked strings, and an oboe sings Down the Petersky Road. The nursemaids’ tune is an old Russian song. It starts modestly, then passes to the horns and spreads through the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 104 onwards, rehearsals 90–99; the song and its transfer from oboe to horns are identified in Gerald Larner’s programme note. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nijinsky behind the mask
cues.text: At the first performance, in Paris on 13 June 1911, Nijinsky dances Petrushka and Tamara Karsavina the Ballerina. Pierre Monteux conducts. Benois supplies the sets and costumes, and Fokine choreographs the puppets and their enormous crowd.
cues.evidence: IRCAM’s work record gives the première date, cast, conductor, designer and choreographer. https://resources.ircam.fr/en/work/petrouchka

cues.title: A pipe and a bear
cues.text: The crowd makes room for a peasant with a performing bear. High clarinets play the peasant’s pipe; a solo tuba answers as the animal, heavy and ungainly. The two voices are several octaves apart.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 115, rehearsal 100, Sostenuto; Gerald Larner describes the pipe and bear’s instrumental voices. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Banknotes in the crowd
cues.text: A merchant arrives with two women dancers, throws banknotes to the crowd and plays his accordion. Benois’s fair has room for money as well as magic. This attraction buys its audience.
cues.evidence: Original stage directions, rehearsals 102–107, transcribed in Kirchmeyer, K012. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

cues.title: The coachmen plant their feet
cues.text: Clarinets and horns repeat a heavy pattern over tuba and timpani. The strings answer with chords marked pesante. These are the coachmen and grooms; when the nursemaids join them, the dance gains another tune without losing its tread.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 126, rehearsal 108, Moderato; the nursemaids join at rehearsal 112. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The 1911 score, before the revision
cues.text: This recording plays Stravinsky’s original 1911 score. After the second tableau the piano scarcely appears again. When he rescored the ballet in 1946–47, he cut back the woodwinds and brass and gave the piano considerably more to play.
cues.evidence: Steven Ledbetter’s Boston Symphony note on the piano’s role in the original and the 1946–47 reorchestration; the London CS 6009 sleeve calls this recording the Original Edition. https://www.bso.org/works/stravinsky-petrushka-1947-version https://archive.org/metadata/lp_petrushka-complete-ballet-original-editio_igor-stravinsky-lorchestre-de-la-suisse-ro

cues.title: Masks in Bengal light
cues.text: The masqueraders arrive by the glow of Bengal lights. Flutes trade quick phrases above celesta and two harps, then strings and clarinets pick up the running figures. Death himself appears among the masks and invites the crowd to dance.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 139–140, rehearsal 117, Agitato. The lighting and Death’s invitation appear in the original scenario transcribed by Kirchmeyer. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cries from the theatre
cues.text: Muted trumpets and cornets cry out from the puppet theatre. Petrushka runs into the fair, pursued by the Moor; the Ballerina tries to hold his attacker back. The dance breaks into a chase.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 150–152, rehearsals 125–128, and the accompanying stage directions. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Snow begins to fall
cues.text: Petrushka falls with his head broken. The music slows to Lento: two piccolos call softly above divided violas, and a clarinet sings a tender little phrase. Snow begins to fall as the crowd gathers around him.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 153–154, rehearsal 129; clarinet marked dolcissimo. The snowfall is specified in the original scenario, transcribed in Kirchmeyer, K012. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Only wood and sawdust
cues.text: A policeman fetches the magician. He picks up Petrushka’s body and shakes it, showing the crowd that it is a wooden puppet stuffed with sawdust. The crowd disperses.
cues.evidence: Original stage directions at rehearsals 129–130 (policeman sent for the Charlatan; he lifts and shakes the body; the crowd disperses), transcribed in Kirchmeyer, K012; the sawdust in Steven Ledbetter’s Boston Symphony note. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka https://www.bso.org/works/stravinsky-petrushka-1947-version

cues.title: The puppet answers back
cues.text: The magician has shown the crowd a lifeless doll. Now Petrushka’s shadow appears above the theatre, thumbing its nose: two trumpets with metal mutes give him back his cry. The magician flees. A few plucked string notes close the ballet.
cues.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 155–156, rehearsals 131–132 and theatrical ending; piccolo trumpet in D and second trumpet in B♭, with metal mutes. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Bassoons prepare the song
transitions.how: At Allegretto, busy bassoon figures and plucked strings replace the crowd’s full orchestra. Solo violins try out scraps of the tune before the oboe sings it. Repeated cello notes keep a small, steady pulse beneath the song.

transitions.title: Clarinets pipe above the bear
transitions.how: The crowd scatters. At Sostenuto, two high clarinets pipe in octaves above slowly stepping bassoons and low strings. The solo tuba answers their tune from far below, its clumsy imitation carrying the bear across the stage.
transitions.evidence: Édition Russe score, pp. 114–115, rehearsal 100; the pipe-and-bear interpretation is also described by Larner. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://geraldlarner.com/work/stravinsky-petrushka-1911

transitions.title: Tuba and timpani set the tread
transitions.how: The merchant’s party withdraws. Moderato begins the coachmen’s dance with repeated low notes in tuba and timpani. Clarinets and horns rock above them, then the strings add their heavy chords, marked pesante.
transitions.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 126, rehearsal 108; preceding departure at rehearsal 107. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

transitions.title: Celesta and harps light the masks
transitions.how: The coachmen’s massed dance breaks into Agitato. Flutes exchange short phrases while celesta and two harps play repeated notes between them. Plucked cellos and second violins enter below; the heavy brass is gone from this first glimpse of the masks.

transitions.title: The trumpets stop the dance
transitions.to: F · Cries from the puppet theatre
transitions.how: The orchestra’s repeated dance chords stop, leaving a muted trumpet call hanging in the air. A second trumpet joins it, then the cornets. The score broadens with Poco allargando before the puppets’ chase bursts onto the fairground.

transitions.title: A tambourine falls to the floor
transitions.from: F · Cries from the puppet theatre
transitions.how: The strings sweep upwards in glissandi as Petrushka is struck. A percussionist drops a tambourine close to the floor. At Lento, two soft piccolos and divided violas remain around the fallen puppet; clarinets join them in short, quiet phrases.
transitions.evidence: Édition Russe score, p. 153, into rehearsal 129; tambourine instruction: hold it close to the floor and let it fall. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: Muted trumpets bring Petrushka back
transitions.how: The departing crowd leaves soft horn figures and oboe notes behind. A piccolo trumpet in D, fitted with a metal mute, cuts across them; the second trumpet answers. Their arpeggios recall the puppet’s cry from his room while the low strings stay silent.

source.title: Stravinsky, Petrushka, 1911 orchestration; Édition Russe plate R.M.V. 127, Dover reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 96–156, rehearsals 82–132; theatrical ending, not alternative p. 150a. Public-domain score in the US, not the EU. Passage timings are provisional, guided by cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-evening.txt. Both harps share one stage position; piccolo trumpet remains under trumpets. Groups vary within each passage.

timeline.note: The curtain passage leads back to massed fairground music.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 96–103, rehearsals 82–89; rapid opening rise and sustained activity through 0:35.

timeline.note: Bassoon figures and plucked strings underpin the nursemaids’ melodic entries.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 104, rehearsal 90; changes at 1:04 and 1:08 followed by a quieter span.

timeline.note: High clarinets and low tuba represent the pipe and bear over a steady low accompaniment.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 115, rehearsal 100; 3:46 boundary and low spectral centroids through 4:25.

timeline.note: The merchant’s dance brings violin flourishes, oboe writing, harp patterns and plucked strings.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 120–121, rehearsals 103–104; relative level rises at 4:45–5:05 after the 4:34 change. Exact dancer entrance remains unaligned.

timeline.note: The coachmen’s opening pattern is deliberately heavy and measured.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 126, rehearsal 108; strongest detected change at 6:08 and lower-centred renewed activity.

timeline.note: The combined dance grows into a larger wind, brass and string texture.
timeline.evidence: Rehearsals 112–116; boundary at 7:42 inside the broad, high-level 7:30–8:15 crest. Groups are passage-level, not a simultaneous inventory.

timeline.note: Quick figures and changing instrumental combinations animate the masqueraders.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 140–144, rehearsals 117–120; 8:26 change before renewed growth and high attack density.

timeline.note: Muted brass cries give way to the chase’s wind, xylophone and string gestures.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 150–153, rehearsals 125–128; changes at 9:48 and 9:54 followed by high brightness at 10:00–10:10. Individual cries and blows are not aligned.

timeline.note: Soft high winds and muted strings replace the violent action.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 153–154, rehearsal 129; abrupt fall to approximately −33 dB at 10:40–10:50.

timeline.note: Low, separated exchanges accompany the Charlatan’s explanation and the dispersing crowd.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 154–155, rehearsal 130; sparse attacks and low relative levels across 11:35–12:00. The stage gestures are not individually timed.

timeline.note: Two metal-muted trumpets carry the shadow’s defiance over the remaining thin texture.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 155–156, rehearsals 131–132; level and brightness rise at 12:35–12:55.

timeline.note: The theatrical ending withdraws into sparse pizzicato string gestures.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 156, after rehearsal 132; 13:02 boundary followed by very low levels through 803.2 seconds.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying 1911 composition and original 1912 score are public domain in the United States; the ordinary EU life-plus-70 composition term has not expired.
fields.note: Stravinsky died in 1971, giving an ordinary EU term through 31 December 2041. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance, and it does not grant rights in modern editions, stage designs or choreography. The viewable score is hosted in the US; recording-term eligibility below does not clear the underlying composition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — first lawful publication anywhere before 1963: London CS 6009, commercially published by 1958. Territorial EU sound-recording basis only; US sound-recording status is not established.
fields.note: A contemporary London/Pecar Electronics advertisement in the Grosse Pointe News, 6 November 1958, p. 7, pictures this Petrushka/Ansermet cover with catalogue CS 6009 under recordings NOW AVAILABLE. This directly establishes commercial availability in 1958; Archive’s 1958 carrier date and Decca’s ℗ 1958 attribution corroborate it. The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication; the US advertisement is therefore pertinent. A 1958 lawful publication exhausted the former 50-year EU performance/phonogram term by the end of 2008, before the 1 November 2013 protection threshold for the 70-year extension. The exact earliest market/day and any earlier issue are not established or required for this pre-1963 finding. No CC licence, worldwide public-domain claim, or US recording clearance is asserted.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: He could make a roomful of dancers lose their footing with one displaced accent, then write a psalm that scarcely moves.
facts: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes · Ramuz’s travelling theatre · Balanchine · Auden and Kallman
Ballets, operas, symphonies and sacred music; composing and recording into his eighties
composer.background:
In St Petersburg, opera was the family business. Stravinsky’s father, Fyodor, sang bass at the Mariinsky Theatre; Igor heard him on stage and began piano lessons at nine. Born in 1882 at Oranienbaum, he entered St Petersburg University to study law. There he befriended Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father heard his first pieces in 1902. Rimsky-Korsakov took him on privately, giving regular lessons from 1905 until his death in 1908. The pupil orchestrated pages of Pan Voyevoda, then had to explain why his teacher had scored them differently.

He married his cousin Catherine Nossenko in 1906; by 1914 they had four children. His E♭ Symphony owed much to Glazunov and Tchaikovsky; Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks showed what he could do with an orchestra in a few minutes. Sergei Diaghilev heard his music in 1909 and gave him some Chopin to orchestrate for Les Sylphides. Then came a whole ballet, The Firebird. Stravinsky handed over the score in sections while Michel Fokine worked out the dances. In his 1936 autobiography he remembered the rehearsals ending with dinner beside Diaghilev and Nijinsky, and good claret.
